comments.text_zh: 我想补充一点：在美国，主要并不是宪法在保护其自由，而是政府结构，以及它如何被设计成让所有相关方之间形成僵局（虽说近来这一特性并没有被保存得太好）。Antonin Scalia 在参议院司法委员会的一次露面中把这一点解释得非常好：[VIDEO] 我承认自己并不完全理解欧盟体系的复杂之处，但表面上看，它在试图通过这类大刀阔斧的立法时，摩擦确实要低得多。
comments.text: I wanted to add that, in the US, it isn't primarily the constitution that protects its freedoms, but rather the structure of their government and how it's been setup for gridlock among all the parties involved (not that that property has been preserved too well of late). Antonin Scalia explained it really well in one of his appearances in front of a Senate Judiciary Committee: [VIDEO] I admit to not fully understanding the intricacies of the EU system but, on the surface, it does appear to be setup for much lower friction when attempting to pass sweeping legislation like this one.

comments.author: ethn
comments.why_zh: Scalia 谈宪法保障的局限
comments.quote_zh: Scalia 对此有过一次很好的演讲
comments.text_zh: 一个受宪法限制的政府也可能明确伤害少数群体的权利，比如美利坚联盟国宪法；或者通过解释和执行，借直接民主程序背离原则的本意。在直接民主中，你确实会得到多数人的暴政，而在代议制民主中这当然会被缓解；比如 2016 年大选，如果按普选票来选，会选出另一位总统。美国建国者对亚里士多德非常熟悉，亚里士多德说过：“不受限制的民主，就像寡头制一样，是一种蔓延到大量人身上的暴政。”确实，美国建国者的决定反映了这一点——如果我们相信他们自己的评论的话。他们选择共和制，动机是人人享有自由，并强调选举结构。1787 年制宪会议上 Hamilton 说：“我们现在正在建立一个共和政府……真正的自由既不存在于专制中，也不存在于民主的极端中，而存在于温和的政府中。”Scalia 对此有过一次很好的演讲，讲的是一个仅仅受宪法限制的政府，在保障其条款、解释和执行方面完全无效：[VIDEO] “每个香蕉共和国都有一部权利法案”
comments.text: A constitutionally limited government can explicitly hurt minority rights, for instance the Confederate States Constitution, or betray intentions of principles through direct democratic procedures by interpretation and enforcement. With direct democracy you do have tyranny of the majority while this is certainly mitigated in a representative democracy; for instance the 2016 election where the popular vote would have selected a different president. The US founding fathers were very familiar with Aristotle who stated: "Unlimited democracy is, just like oligarchy, a tyranny spread over a large number of people.” Indeed the US founding fathers' decisions reflect this, If we're to believe their commentary, they picked a republic with the motivation of liberty for all with emphasis on the elective structure, Constitutional Convention of Hamilton 1787 : "We are now forming a republican government...Real liberty is neither found in despotism or the extremes of democracy, but in moderate governments.” Scalia has a good talk about this, how a merely constitutionally limited government is completely ineffective of guaranteeing its provisions, its interpretation, and its enforcements: [VIDEO] "Every banana republic has a bill of rights"

comments.text_zh: 我很想在这里和其他人讨论一件相关的事。最近（令我意外的是）我被 YouTube 上 Antonin Scalia 的一些演讲吸引了。多年前，他站在我认为在社会上公正且良善的判决的反面，这让我感到反感（或者对他孤身一人感到好笑）；如今我远不再这样，而是开始更好地理解他在做什么。至少如果你相信他的演讲的话。听完他的演讲（再回想他的意见）后，我明白他是在努力确保宪法被严格按照法律条文来遵循；如果人民对它不满，就让他们去修改它，使它反映民众的意愿。但要让这一过程按程序进行。而不是让社会或政治意愿通过个别法官或法院的裁定悄悄渗入——即判定某件事如今已经“足够可接受”，以至于可以裁定它已经演变、在当下符合宪法。而且宪法制定者既是在努力防止灾难，也是在努力促成进步——当我们偏离那些编码了这一目标的文字时，就应该小心，因为一旦那样做，就会打开各种意想不到的后果。（因此这和楼主的故事以及关于把法律当作源代码的评论有关。）这真的让我大开眼界，明白了司法保守主义的这一面向究竟是怎么回事。这并不是说我同意它的全部哲学，或同意它（在政治上）讨好某一类选民的倾向。但它确实在我心中激起了
comments.text: I'd love to discuss with others here something related. I have lately (to my surprise) been drawn by some talks of Antonin Scalia on Youtube. Far from being repelled (or amused at his standing alone) as I was years ago by his coming down on the opposite side of judgements I thought were socially just and good, I now come to understand better what he was doing. At least if you believe his talks. After listening to his talks (and then thinking back to his opinions), I understand he was trying to make sure that the Constitution was followed to the letter of the law, and that if the people were unhappy with it, let them change it so that it reflected the popular desires. But let it follow that process. Not have social or political will creep its way in via individual judges' or courts' determination something was now "acceptable enough" that it could be ruled to have evolved and be constitutional at the present time. And that the writers of the Constitution were trying to prevent disaster as much as trying to enable progress -- and that we should be careful when we stray from the words encoding that goal, because when you do that it opens up all sorts of unintended consequences. (Hence the connection to this OP's story + comments about law as source code.) This really opened my eyes about what that aspect of judicial conservatism is about. Not that I agree with all of its philosophy or tendency (in politics) to court a certain sector of the vote, for example. But it did arouse in

comments.quote_zh: 但是，看过 Scalia 之后，你怎么可能不喜欢他？
comments.text_zh: 完全正确！这正是这段对话如此有意思的原因——也正是为什么他们看起来被不公平地踩了。「友谊是否会随着时间推移损害系统的完整性？」这个问题相当引人入胜，而且很多国家都有大量例子表明「是的，确实会」。所以，说也许系统应该以某种方式惩罚友谊，看起来完全站得住脚。但是，看过 Scalia 之后，你怎么可能不喜欢他？[VIDEO] [LINK] 他机智、有魅力，还是个演讲大师。所以当人们听到「不能和 Scalia 做朋友，尽管你和他一起工作」时，感觉有点像「不能呼吸，尽管你是人」。这是个逻辑矛盾。而且这甚至都不是一个定义明确的问题：到底什么是「友谊」？
comments.text: Exactly! Which is why this conversation is so interesting – and why it seemed they were unfairly downvoted. The question of "does friendship compromise integrity of systems over time?" is quite fascinating, and there are many examples across many countries that show "yes, yes it does." So it seemed entirely legitimate to say that perhaps a system should penalize friendships, somehow. But, after watching Scalia, how can you not like him? [VIDEO] [LINK] He was witty, charming, and a master orator. So when people hear "can't have a friendship with Scalia, even though you work with him," it's kind of like "can't breathe, even though you're human." It's a logical contradiction. And it's not even a well-defined problem: what is a "friendship," anyway?

comments.quote_zh: 关于开国元勋为何这样设计制度，最好的解释之一就是已故大法官 Scalia 的这个[1]。
comments.text_zh: 记住，开国元勋们对民主的评价非常低，这就是为什么他们选择建立共和国，然后又通过宪法来限制这个共和国。如果民主党人在人数上处于劣势，他们就会支持共和制，而共和党人就会支持民主制。但是，关于开国元勋为何这样设计制度，最好的解释之一就是已故大法官 Scalia 的这个[1]。基本理念是，美国制度的设计是为了在时间和空间上代表共和国的意志：- 每一项法案都需要众议院、参议院和总统三方通过 - 众议院更替非常快（每2年）- 总统更替速度适中（每4年）- 参议院更替缓慢（每6年，且每2年部分更替）- 众议院代表人口 - 参议院平等代表各州（或者说代表土地）- 总统通过混合制度选出（选举人团，按人口比例分配）。- 基本理念是，任何法案都必须得到以下各方同意：a. 不仅是短期（众议院）的人民意志，还有中期（总统）和长期（参议院）的人民意志。当英国想退出欧盟时，留欧派认为应该重新投票，因为他们不相信人们是在充分了解信息的情况下投票的。当然，多年后通过大选进行的第二次代理投票让意图变得清晰，但在美国，我们不会让一项法案通过，除非它不只是我们投票支持的东西
comments.text: Remember, founding fathers had a very dim view on Democracy, this is why they chose to have a Republic and then restrict the republic through a constitution. If Democrats were losing out to big numbers, they would pro-republic and Republicans would be pro-democracy. But, one of the best explanations for why founding fathers built the system the way they did is this[1], by late Justice Scalia. The fundamental idea is that the American system is created to represent the will of the republic across time and space: - Every bill needs to be passed by all three House, Senate and the President - House recycles very fast (every 2 years) - President recycles at a moderate speed (every 4 years) - Senate recycles at a slow pace (every 6 years, and partially every 2 years) - House represents the population - Senate represents all states equally (or represents land) - Presidency is elected through a hybrid system (electoral college, which is distributed in proportion to the population). - The fundamental idea is that any bill must be agreed upon by: a. The will of the people not just in short term (house), but in mid-term (presidency) and long term (senate) also. When UK wanted out of EU, the remainers believed that they should have a revote because they didn't believe that people voted with full information. Of course, years later a second proxy vote through general elections made the intent clear, but in the US we will not go for a bill to be passed unless its not just what we voted for
